title: [BUG] High RSS Memory Usage Even with Active Defrag
body: Since upgrading our standalone Redis servers from 6.2.5 to 7.2.5, an affected server will occasionally keep growing in RSS until the system is nearly out of memory. Active defragmentation starts running but the RSS remains high. During one occurrence, MEMORY STATS reported about 9.09 GB allocated, 12.53 GB active, 12.67 GB resident, and roughly 3.44 GB of allocator-fragmentation bytes. I captured MEMORY STATS and jemalloc statistics and can collect more data when it happens again.

symptoms_visible: Since upgrading our standalone Redis servers from 6.2.5 to 7.2.5, an affected server occasionally grows in RSS until the system is nearly out of memory.
During an occurrence, active defragmentation runs while MEMORY STATS shows about 9.09 GB allocated, 12.53 GB active, 12.67 GB resident, and about 3.44 GB of allocator-fragmentation bytes.
N0.label: N0 high RSS regression reported

symptoms_visible: I ran MEMORY PURGE during another occurrence, and the server still had about 11.47 GB RSS for 8.46 GB of used memory while active defragmentation was running.
N1_x.label: N1_x memory purge aftermath

symptoms_visible: On 7.2.5, RSS can climb much higher than dataset memory; before the upgrade, memory reached maxmemory and stayed there without this RSS growth.
N2.label: N2 upgrade regression established

symptoms_visible: The intermittent RSS growth continues with active defragmentation enabled and its thresholds at their defaults.
N3.label: N3 defrag configuration collected

symptoms_visible: On a host showing a high fragmentation ratio, the debug log repeatedly reports approximately 2.18 MB allocated, 2.80 MB active, and 5.61 MB resident; that host has not yet run out of memory.
N4.label: N4 debug evidence collected

symptoms_visible: After upgrading to 7.4.5, the recurring RSS memory growth no longer appears on our servers.
N_terminal.label: N_terminal memory issue resolved after upgrade

symptoms_visible: After upgrading to 7.4.5, the recurring RSS memory growth no longer appears on our servers.
N_terminal_x.label: N_terminal_x resolved after purge branch

solution.intent: Ask jemalloc to release unused pages with MEMORY PURGE as the resolution for the excess RSS.
solution.concrete_example: Run MEMORY PURGE while RSS is elevated and check whether the operating-system memory footprint falls back near used_memory.

edges.comment: Reporter c0, on the original reporter's Redis 7.2.5 deployment: the reporter independently ran MEMORY PURGE during a recurrence and then supplied INFO ALL showing RSS still around 11.47 GB for 8.46 GB used memory. This was an actual falsified attempt, not evidence from participant2's separate Redis 6.2 deployment.

question_patterns: What did the memory footprint look like before the Redis upgrade?
Did RSS also climb above dataset memory on 6.2.5?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Before the upgrade, memory would reach maxmemory and stay there. RSS never climbed like this and definitely did not climb much higher than the dataset memory.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The same RSS growth happened regularly on 6.2.5, before the upgrade.
RSS sometimes sat slightly above dataset memory before the upgrade, but it never grew by several gigabytes or threatened system memory.

edges.comment: Participant1 c1 and reporter c2, describing only the original reporter's deployment: the reporter established that this behavior began after moving from 6.2.5 to 7.2.5. The uncompleted --bigkeys request is omitted because no output was ever produced and the maintainer said large keys were unlikely to be related.

question_patterns: What are your active-defragmentation configuration values?
Can you share the defrag-related section of redis.conf?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Our defrag settings are mostly default: activedefrag yes, active-defrag-ignore-bytes 100mb, threshold-lower 10, threshold-upper 100, cycle-min 1, max-scan-fields 1000, and active-defrag-cycle-max is set to 10 instead of the default 25.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I checked the configuration and activedefrag is disabled.
The same settings are in use except active-defrag-cycle-max is still at its default value of 25.

edges.comment: Participant1 c16 and reporter c17, on the original reporter's Redis 7.2.5 servers: the reporter pasted the active-defragmentation configuration. The threshold discussion in c6-c13 belongs to participant2's independent Redis 6.2.18 system and is deliberately not folded into this causal chain.

question_patterns: Can you enable DEBUG logging during an occurrence and share the relevant allocator lines?
When this happens again, please collect debug logs showing allocated, active, resident, and fragmentation values.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I enabled debug logging and captured a sample from a host currently showing a high fragmentation ratio, although it was not out of memory yet. The repeated lines are around allocated=2180016, active=2797568, resident=5611520, frag=28%, with roughly 618 KB of fragmentation bytes and 3.43 MB of RSS bytes.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: During the real high-RSS event, the debug logs show allocated, active, and resident staying nearly equal while RSS growth comes from outside jemalloc.
The timestamps and client source ports differ, but the allocator values are the same.

edges.comment: Participant1 c16 and reporter c18-c20, on the original reporter's fleet: the reporter supplied raw DEBUG allocator lines from a host with elevated fragmentation but explicitly noted that it had not yet exhausted memory. The maintainer considered that sample's ratio reasonable at its low absolute memory use; no stronger conclusion is put into the user's answer.

solution.intent: Treat the high RSS as the Redis active-defragmentation regression affecting the expires dictionary, upgrade to a release containing the corrected defrag traversal, and ask the reporter to verify memory behavior under the same workload.
solution.concrete_example: Upgrade from the affected 7.2.5 deployment to a fixed build such as 7.4.5. The identified bug could leave the current database's expires dictionary making only minimal progress because a defragmentation cycle could exit after finishing keys instead of allowing the keys and expires scans to finish. Monitor the upgraded servers for several days under their normal eviction and expiration workload before declaring the issue resolved.
solution.inference_hint: The maintainer's research in c21-c22 identified the accepted mechanism: an active-defragmentation regression allowed a cycle to leave after keys were defragmented without waiting for the current database's keys and expires work to finish. With many expired-key entries, db->expires could therefore be processed only once per cycle and take an extremely long time to complete. This conclusion is engineer-side inference and is not something the reporter derived from the raw logs.

edges.comment: Participant1 c21-c24 identified the regression and the already-available fixed upgrade path for the original reporter's 7.2.5 deployment. Reporter c23, c25, and c26 installed 7.4.5, observed improvement over several days, and finally confirmed that the memory issue appeared addressed. Backport scheduling and pull-request identifiers are not scored.

solution.intent: Move past the ineffective purge and upgrade to a release containing the correction for active defragmentation leaving the expires scan too early, then verify the result under the normal workload.
solution.concrete_example: MEMORY PURGE does not address this case. Upgrade the affected server to a fixed build such as 7.4.5, then monitor RSS through the workload pattern that previously triggered the growth and confirm whether it remains controlled.
solution.inference_hint: This shortcut represents giving the ultimately correct upgrade recommendation immediately after the reporter demonstrates that MEMORY PURGE does not reduce the excess RSS. The exact expires-dictionary early-exit mechanism was discovered by the maintainer and must be presented as engineering diagnosis rather than as user-provided evidence.

edges.comment: Recovery from reporter c0's falsified MEMORY PURGE attempt to the accepted resolution in c21-c26. This shortcut skips later configuration and debug-log collection but retains the actual reporter-confirmed outcome after upgrading.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause: the affected Redis active-defragmentation logic could exit a cycle after processing keys without allowing the current database's expires scan to finish, so a large expires dictionary could make extremely slow progress and leave substantial allocator fragmentation and RSS.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the observed post-upgrade regression, the large allocated-versus-active gap, active defragmentation already running, and the reporter's defrag configuration; it must not be inferred from participant2's unrelated Redis 6.2 deployment.
Must recommend upgrading to a build containing the corrected active-defragmentation traversal rather than treating MEMORY PURGE as the resolution.
Must not claim that MEMORY PURGE fixes the issue; the original reporter ran it during an occurrence and the high RSS remained.
Must ask the reporter to monitor and verify the result on a build containing the fix under the workload that previously triggered the RSS growth before declaring resolution.
Resolution is confirmed only by the original reporter's post-upgrade observation that the recurring memory issue no longer appears.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced Redis operator managing standalone production servers; comfortable collecting INFO ALL, MEMORY STATS, jemalloc statistics, configuration excerpts, and DEBUG logs, but relies on maintainers for source-level diagnosis.
persona_hint.communication_style: Polite, patient, and evidence-oriented. Provides large diagnostic dumps when requested, follows up when investigation stalls, distinguishes tentative improvement from confirmed resolution, and verifies changes over several days.
